title: Great things while small
hookLine: do the difficult while it's easy, the great while it's small (Tao Te Ching 63)

lines: THE SAGE NEVER REACHES FOR THE GREAT.
cards: Here's a puzzle from chapter sixty-three of the Tao Te Ching: the sage never sets out to do anything great, and great things get done anyway. How? A shoelace gives a clue.
Pick at a knot the moment it snags, and it comes loose with a fingernail. Walk on it all day, and by evening it needs a pin and some patience. Same knot, very different job.
Back on day nine hundred seventy-six, this chapter gave you a small word, xi. Today it goes further: meet great and difficult things before they're either.

teach.h: THE HARD THING, WHILE IT'S EASY.
teach.b: First, the line. Plan for what's difficult while it's still easy; do what's great while it's still small. Legge's translation puts it as the master who anticipates things that are difficult while they are easy.
The hard part is mostly timing. Second, where hard things come from.
The difficult things in the world all begin as easy ones, the chapter says, and the great things as small ones. Nothing arrives full-size. The argument in the car started as a sigh at breakfast.
The debt started as one charge. Third, back to the puzzle.
The sage never sets out to do great things, and that's exactly how great things get done: not by heroic pushes, but by quiet attention to small ones, again and again.
The same chapter folds in a line about meeting harm itself. In Legge's words, the way is "to recompense injury with kindness." A grudge, too, is easier to settle while it's small.
Fourth, a warning about lightness. Easy promises earn little trust, the chapter says, and treating many things as easy brings many difficulties.

teach.h: TREAT IT AS HARD, AND IT ISN'T.
teach.b: So the sage treats things as hard, and in the end finds nothing hard. That means taking the small thing seriously now, the email, the apology, the loose knot, before it grows into the one that takes the whole weekend.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-three as everyday advice: deal with problems early, while they are small, and take small things seriously.

games.q: what does “great things while small” mean?
o: waiting for small chances to turn into big ones
only taking on tasks small enough to finish fast
doing the hard thing early, before it has grown

s: chapter sixty-three says the sage takes on great projects
it says the sage never sets out to do great things, and so great things get done.
the chapter says easy promises earn little trust
it warns that treating things lightly brings many difficulties.

games.q: a small problem shows up: a snagged lace, a misunderstanding, a late bill. according to chapter sixty-three, when do you deal with it?
o: now, while it's small and easy.
once it's big enough to matter.
games.why: the chapter says to plan for the difficult while it's easy and do the great while it's small, because hard things start as easy ones.

practice: Let your mind run over the week the way fingers run along a lace, feeling for a snag: a message you haven't answered, a small tension with someone, a bill, a loose step.
Choose one that's still just a loose knot, and look at it plainly. Find the first easy move, the fingernail, not the pin.

wordCard.voice: Great things while small. Chapter sixty-three's advice: do the difficult while it's easy, and the great while it's small. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: while it's small. The fingernail beats the pin, every time it's caught early. Until tomorrow.
